# Cātuma Sutta (MN 67 (PTS MN i 456))

**ID:** MN 67 (PTS MN i 456)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Cātuma Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** At Cātumā
**PTS:** MN i 456
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn67
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cātuma Sutta* (MN 67; PTS MN i 456), titled *At Cātumā* in English, is set in a myrobalan grove at the Śākyan town of Cātumā [Tan 2002/2004; SuttaCentral]. When five hundred newly ordained visiting monks arrive under the charge of the chief disciples Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna and create a commotion while greeting resident monks, the Buddha inquires of Ānanda regarding the noise and summarily dismisses the unruly assembly [Tan 2002/2004; Freedman 1977; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. After intercession by local Śākyans and Brahmā Sahampati, the Buddha relents [Freedman 1977; SuttaCentral]. Questioning his chief disciples about their reaction to the dismissal, the Buddha rebukes Sāriputta for assuming the Master wished to rest and that the disciples should do likewise, while commending Moggallāna for recognizing that leadership and pastoral care of the Saṅgha devolved onto the chief disciples [Tan 2002/2004; Freedman 1977; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The Buddha subsequently delivers a discourse on four perils confronting a monastic who has entered the religious life, framed through water imagery: the peril of waves (anger and irritability), alligators (gluttony and lack of restraint regarding food), whirlpools (the five cords of sensual pleasure), and sharks (women, exemplified by a monk who wanders on almsround without established mindfulness and disrobes after encountering an alluring woman) [Freedman 1977; Hazra 1994; Anālayo 2003; Wayman 1997].

SuttaCentral notes full parallels in the Chinese Ekottarika Āgama (EĀ 45.2), an individual translation in the Taishō canon (T 137), the *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4.122), and the *Yasoja Sutta* of the Udāna (Ud 3.3; PTS Ud 24), alongside a partial parallel in SN 22.80 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial Pali-internal text reuse, aligning the four hazards (§14.2–18.5) closely with AN 4.122 (§122.1.1–122.4.5_1) and the opening narrative (§2.1–5.2) with Ud 3.3 (§1.3–5.1_1), while also finding matches in SN 22.80, MN 29, and Vinaya Khandhaka texts (Kd 1 and Kd 17) [DharmaNexus]. In Ud 3.3, a closely parallel dismissal narrative takes place at Sāvatthī with monks led by Yasoja rather than the chief disciples [Freedman 1977; Masefield 1997]. DharmaNexus also aligns the text cross-linguistically with EĀ 45.2 (T 125, fascicle 41) and T 137 [DharmaNexus]. The episode of the dismissal and pacification is discussed in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 5.3.12 and Mil 5.4.10) [Freedman 1977; SuttaCentral]. English translations have been published by I.B. Horner and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
